items.title: Japan targets 35 shadow fleet ships in first vessel sanctions
items.original_title: Japan targets 35 shadow fleet ships in first vessel sanctions
items.summary: Japan has imposed sanctions directly on individual vessels for the first time, targeting 35 ships linked to Russia’s shadow fleet as Tokyo steps up efforts to restrict Moscow’s oil-export network. The measures took effect on October 2 under Japan’s Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act. Japanese companies will now need government permission to provide specified services to the 35 vessels and for capital transactions, including loans and debt guarantees, connected with their sale, purchase, lease or charter. Japan’s foreign ministry has identified all 35 ships by IMO number. It is the first time Tokyo has placed vessels themselves under sanctions, bringing Japan closer to the approach already adopted by the UK and European Union against ageing tankers moving Russian oil outside mainstream Western shipping, finance and insurance channels. The shipping measures formed part of a wider package that also froze the assets of 33 Russian organisations and nine individuals and introduced export restrictions against four entities in Turkey and the UAE. Tokyo said the vessel measures were aimed at ships being used to transport Russian crude and petroleum products while circumventing existing sanctions. Seventy-two of those ships subsequently transported an estimated €7.5bn ($8.8bn) of Russian fossil fuels. Clarksons data showed the Russian registry up 38.2% this year through September 1.

items.title: Oil exports surge back through Hormuz despite mounting attacks
items.original_title: Oil exports surge back through Hormuz despite mounting attacks
items.summary: Oil flows from the Middle East have climbed back above pre-war levels even as attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz accelerate to their fastest pace since the conflict with Iran erupted on February 28. Provisional Kpler data shows regional crude exports exceeded pre-war volumes on four days during the final week of September, reaching between 19.5m and 22.5m barrels per day. The seven-day moving average stood at 18.5m barrels per day on October 1, compared with an average of around 18m barrels per day in the year before the war. The numbers cover Hormuz and Red Sea movements as well as terminal exports and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Iraqi Oil Tankers Company has transported a 2m-barrel cargo through Hormuz on a chartered VLCC, taking responsibility for the crude beyond the strait rather than selling it on the traditional free-on-board basis at Basra. The surge in cargoes transiting Hormuz is being matched, however, by an equally sharp escalation in attacks. The 115,100 dwt Lipsi, operated by Greece’s Dynacom Tankers Management, was hit by an unknown projectile in Hormuz on Sunday, suffering engine-room damage. Off Yemen, the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Chrystal Sky reported several explosions around 60 nautical miles south of Al Mukha on Sunday.

items.title: Where freight forwarders actually lose money
items.original_title: Where freight forwarders actually lose money
items.summary: More often than not, a forwarder closes a clean month and still watches the margins come in light. Most forwarders already know where it went: into the charges that were never recovered and the costs that were never meant to happen. A demurrage charge that was never passed on to the customer. Forwarders already have more data than they can read. Everything after is just a record of money already gone. So, the job is narrower than what most tech pitches: flag the handful of shipments where an unexpected charge is about to be incurred, whether that is demurrage building, a customs delay, port congestion that holds up haulage, or a misinterpreted contract, and put them in front of the operator early enough for them to act. Command Center surfaces the risks, the AI agents take routine tracking and reconciling off the operator’s plate, and Freight Audit checks carrier invoices against the contract and the actual shipment, so overcharges and miscalculated D&D are caught before they are paid rather than written off after. BCOs are already benchmarking their forwarders on exactly that, and it is often the difference between an account that renews and one that goes out to tender. For most forwarders, the honest answer is uncomfortable, and it is also the easiest money they will find all year.

Members are encouraged to continue following established bunker testing and fuel management practices and to make use of Neptune’s fuel quality intelligence when evaluating supply risks and preparing bunkering plans. For non-producers, which include traders and refineries with capacities of less than 1 million metric tons/year, the ban will remain in place until the end of January. The deputy prime minister added that given Russia produces more diesel than it consumes, it is necessary to avoid accumulating more stocks than the country has the capacity to store, which would force refineries to reduce throughput and affect the output of other products. Novak’s comments come a day after Russia’s President Vladimir Putin said at the Valday Forum in Moscow that Russia had sufficient diesel but warned the fuel wouldn’t make it to international markets because of foreign sanctions. AI will be used to support vetting and processing. The move comes after a sharp expansion of the Singapore flag. The Singapore Registry of Ships ended 2025 at a record 137m gt, up 27% year on year, with more than 4,400 vessels on its books. That put Singapore fourth among the world’s largest registries, while its approximately 11-year average fleet age was the youngest among the top 10 flags. Singapore has also been tightening registry oversight. Last month MPA warned owners and agents that false or unverifiable vessel identity, ownership, registration and trading information submitted in connection with port calls could trigger enforcement action, against the backdrop of growing concern internationally over fraudulent registries and flag-hopping. Eight methanol-fuelled ships have joined the Singapore flag since 2020, and MPA said the country expects to register its first ammonia dual-fuel vessel in November.

items.title: What Is the Shadow Fleet, and Why Is It So Hard to Count?
items.original_title: What Is the Shadow Fleet, and Why Is It So Hard to Count?
items.summary: There Is No Official Shadow Fleet List The shadow fleet, also called the dark fleet, refers to tankers and support vessels that rely on deceptive shipping practices to move sanctioned or high-risk commodities while concealing their true origin, ownership, or destination. It has no standing in law, and that is where the difficulty starts. Why Every Published Estimate Is Different Ask five organizations how large the shadow fleet is, and you will get five answers, sometimes differing by a factor of three. The useful question is narrower: Does this vessel exhibit the behavior, and what is my exposure if it does? A vessel flying a legitimate flag has the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea, and on the high seas it is subject to the jurisdiction of its flag state. There is a lag between a vessel starting to operate as part of the shadow fleet and that vessel appearing on a sanctions list. During that gap, the vessel is detectable through its behavior and invisible to a list check. Vessels without a valid flag are stateless, and under Article 110 of UNCLOS, a warship may board a ship on the high seas where there are reasonable grounds to suspect it is.

items.summary: The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black and Red Seas, as well as environmental topics, were among the key issues discussed when BIMCO’s Maritime Safety & Security Committee (MSSC) and Marine Environment Committee (MEC) met on 30 September and 1 October. Members considered the implications of regional conflicts, attacks on shipping, drones, mines and navigational disruption. The committees also discussed a broad range of other regulatory, safety and environmental issues affecting the day-to-day operation of ships. Our committees bring together industry expertise to identify practical challenges and help shape BIMCO’s positions in discussions with the IMO, governments and regulators. Digitalisation was another major theme, including the opportunities it offers for efficiency, compliance and safety, as well as the growing importance of cyber security and supporting seafarers as technology develops. Members also discussed the safe adoption of alternative fuels, including ammonia, hydrogen and methanol, and future safety frameworks for advanced modular nuclear reactors. The proposed legally-binding international convention on biofouling was also discussed, with an emphasis on ensuring that future requirements are practical, science-based and capable of consistent implementation across the global fleet. Other topics included search and rescue and mixed migration, underwater radiated noise, marine plastics and plastic pellet transportation, and implementation of the Hong Kong Convention on ship recycling. items.original_title: Clean tanker markets size up impact of potential US diesel export curbs
items.summary: US restrictions on diesel exports would upend Atlantic Basin clean tanker demand at a moment when the global middle-distillate market is reeling from simultaneous supply shocks in Russia and the Middle East, BRS Shipbrokers said in a report. The impact on medium-range tanker earnings in particular could be swift and severe, BRS said Sept. 28. US President Donald Trump had floated a diesel export ban in response to record domestic fuel prices ahead of midterm elections. Tanker implications A full ban could strand around 1.35 million b/d of US Gulf diesel exports — the equivalent of four MR2-sized cargoes per day — with Europe and Latin America most exposed given the absence of readily available alternative supply, BRS said. Pressure would fall most heavily on MR2s, which carry more than 90% of US diesel exports, BRS said. There could also be bleed-in to MR1 markets as MR2s compete for smaller stems, while clean tankers would likely ballast away from the US Gulf, putting pressure on tonnage lists elsewhere, BRS said. The offsetting factor for the broader clean tanker complex is a potential redirection of Asian barrels westward. “With the potential diesel ban coming, the appetite for US diesel exports is declining because these products are needed at home, whether there’s a ban or not,” Simpson said.

items.title: Electric and hybrid ferries could cut emissions by 63% in Sea of Marmara, IMO study finds
items.original_title: Electric and hybrid ferries could cut emissions by 63% in Sea of Marmara, IMO study finds
items.summary: Türkiye’s Sea of Marmara ferry network could cut greenhouse gas emissions by 63% by switching to a mix of hybrid and fully electric vessels, while avoiding nearly half a billion euros in health and environmental damage costs and supporting around 1,100 jobs a year, according to a new IMO study. Commissioned by IMO’s GreenVoyage2050 programme in partnership with Türkiye’s Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure, the study assessed 67 Ro-Ro and Ro-Pax ferries carrying vehicles and passengers across 26 ports. The network transports around 25 million passengers and seven million vehicles each year. Significant potential to cut emissions The study found that battery-electric and hybrid propulsion are technically feasible options across all Ro-Pax and Ro-Ro ferry operations assessed in the Sea of Marmara. It identified an optimum scenario combining hybrid and fully electric vessels to balance emissions reductions and costs. Under this scenario, annual GHG emissions could fall by around 63% by 2050 compared with business-as-usual operations using diesel fuel. The transition would also reduce local air pollution and could avoid an estimated €492 million in cumulative health and environmental damage costs. Going further, converting the entire fleet to fully electric operations could cut GHG emissions by 84% by 2050.

Cabinet has also approved a feasibility study into bringing in a minority equity partner from one of South Africa’s development finance institutions. South Africa’s ports have endured a prolonged period of congestion, equipment shortages, inadequate maintenance and declining productivity. TNPA has also launched private-sector processes covering Cape Town’s multipurpose terminal, a new floating drydock there and the Richards Bay dry bulk terminal, while Transnet last week opened the qualification process for a private partner for the R30bn-R44bn Ngqura manganese corridor.

Suez containership transits rose 59% from March to September, from 139 to 221. The growth came from large ships, 300m and above, up to 24,000 TEU, the post-Panamax to ultra-large vessels used on main Asia-Europe services, which rose from 22 to 127 transits a month. Around 100 more large containerships now transit the Suez Canal instead of around Africa, compared to March, cutting one to two weeks off each round trip. Suez routing for Asia-Europe services has recovered to only about a quarter of pre-crisis levels, per Sea-Intelligence. Even a partial return matters, because carriers expanded Asia-Europe capacity by approximately 41% between May 2023 and May 2025 to cover the longer route around Africa, according to Alphaliner, meaning that every service that switches back to Suez frees ships the route no longer needs. Shorter voyages mean each liner service needs fewer ships to keep its schedule, freeing capacity just as Europe-bound demand softens after the summer and ahead of China’s Golden Week holiday (1-7 Oct), when factory closures halt much of China’s export production.

These moments tend to be fleeting and have historically been associated with the hottest stages of shipping cycles. The question is how often the market has reached this altitude before, and how long it can survive there. The previous maximum premium for a five-year-old VLCC over a newbuild was 21% in December 2007. Veson data shows a 15-year-old VLCC overtook the newbuild value for the first time on September 27. Danish Ship Finance takes a broader approach, using a monthly secondhand-to-newbuilding price ratio for tankers stretching back to January 2000. Its series identifies 11 distinct episodes, including the current one. “To stay with your analogy: the death zone usually punishes those who linger — but in 2003–08, the market camped up there for nearly six years,” Danish Ship Finance told Splash. Photo courtesy CMA CGM Alternative-fuel ship orders rebounded sharply in the third quarter, with September delivering the strongest monthly total in nearly two years as LNG remained the dominant choice for new vessels. Shipowners placed orders for 69 alternative-fuelled vessels in September, the highest monthly total since October 2024, according to new figures from DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight platform. The September activity brought third-quarter orders to 168 vessels, making it the busiest quarter since the third quarter of 2024. “September capped the strongest quarter for alternative-fuelled vessel contracting in the past two years, bringing year-to-date orders comfortably above the level seen at the same point last year.” LNG accounted for 48 of September’s 69 orders, covering containerships, car carriers, bulk carriers and ro-ro cargo vessels. Another 12 orders were for ethanol-fuelled bulk carriers, while nine LPG-fuelled vessels were ordered during the month. DNV warned in its latest Maritime Forecast to 2050 that regulatory outcomes could significantly change the economics of alternative fuels over the operating lives of vessels ordered today. Alternative-fuel-capable tonnage has already grown from just 0.4% of the global fleet in 2020 to 5.2% in 2026, according to DNV, led primarily by LNG and methanol systems.

items.summary: The Coast Guard, Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, Newark Fire Department, and multiple state and area agencies respond to a fire in Port Newark on the vehicle carrier ship, Grande Costa D’Avorio. Fire fighting crews are working to extinguish the fire both from the pier and from FDNY fireboats. (U.S. Coast Guard photo by Dan Henry) A new federal watchdog report says gaps in training, coordination and emergency planning continue to complicate the response to ship fires at U.S. The Government Accountability Office report found 886 nearshore marine fires were reported to the U.S. gCaptain covered the firefighting response at the time . The Coast Guard established a National Salvage and Marine Firefighting Task Force in January 2024 and has since developed online training and other tools. GAO said Coast Guard officials and marine firefighting providers described a broader “wait and see” problem in which vessel operators may hesitate to activate response plans because of the expense associated with mobilizing commercial firefighting and salvage resources. The watchdog also issued five recommendations to the Coast Guard, including assigning marine firefighting coordination duties to specific field personnel, working with local fire departments to arrange vessel tours and exercises, creating a system for sharing lessons and best practices, and providing clearer guidance on when vessel response plans should be activated.

items.original_title: U.S. Ports Push Nuclear Power, Faster Dredging at Record AAPA Convention
items.summary: By Tom Ewing (gCaptain) – The American Association of Port Authorities wrapped up its annual convention in New Orleans on Wednesday after drawing its largest attendance ever, with more than 900 participants representing over 90 ports.
